confidence_note: Gates mosquito jar is well documented (Nature, Gallo's pieces, Kirkus names it as a book example). Mehrabian and '200 hours' from the old text were rejected. The Gates quote wording varies, so no direct quotation is used. Gallo's less-than-five-percent figure comes from his own site.
facts: At TED in February 2009 (Long Beach), Bill Gates spoke about malaria and opened a jar of mosquitoes on stage, saying malaria is spread by mosquitoes and he had brought some.
The Gates Foundation later said the mosquitoes were not carrying the disease; Gallo says Gates told the audience so only after the stunt had grabbed attention.
The talk ran 18 minutes; Gallo says the mosquito segment took up less than five percent of Gates's speaking time.
Gallo calls it a jaw-dropping moment, says every presentation needs one, and links it to what neuroscientists call an emotionally charged event.
Neuroscientist A. K. Pradeep says the brain is wired to notice what is new and stands out.
Gallo advises soft breaks (stories, videos, demonstrations) every ten minutes in a longer talk.
Gallo describes the room going silent, then laughing and applauding.
scene_details: A glass jar opened on a stage.
Under five percent of an eighteen-minute talk.
tension: Gates used a few seconds of a long talk on something the audience could not ignore.
opening_idea: Open on the jar being opened.

lessons.idea: One physical moment can carry a whole subject.
lessons.anchor: The mosquito jar in an eighteen-minute malaria talk.

reflect_final: What single object or action could you put in front of people so that the point of your next explanation sticks?

use_cases.situation: Training a new team on a safety rule
use_cases.move: Gates held up a jar of mosquitoes; I'll bring the real object instead of describing it.

use_cases.situation: Teaching a child about saving water
use_cases.move: Fill a bucket with what a leaking tap wastes and let them see it.
